# Warlord Era

in Brill's Encyclopedia of China Online

Author:

Edward A. McCord

Edward A. McCord Search for other papers by Edward A. McCord in Current site Google Scholar

(1,041 words)

The Warlord period, usually dated from 1916 to 1927, refers to a time of political disunity in China when competing military commanders dominated society and government by virtue of their command of military force. The Warlord period was foreshadowed in the late 19th century by the rise to political influence of regional army commanders who assisted the Qing dynasty in the defeat of the Taiping Rebellion and other major rebellions. Unlike the near political autonomy of 20th century warlords, though, these commanders remained subordinate to the central state. The immediate context for the rise of warlordism was a lack of consensus following the Revolution of 1911 over fundamental political issues, such as the relative powers of executive and legislative branches, and the relationship between national, provincial, and local governments. Military force was ultimately applied to resolve these issues in a series of civil wars. Rather than leading to any lasting political solution, though, these wars simply increased the autonomous political power of the military commanders at the head of provincial or regional armies who fought in them. The result was the political fragmentation of the nation among these competing "warlords."

The Warlord period is conventionally dated as beginning in 1916 with the death of Yuan Shikai, second president of the Chinese Republic (1912-49). A proponent of strong executive power and centralized bureaucratic government, Yuan used his control over China's largest military force, the Beiyang Army, to maintain some degree of national unity. Following Yuan's death in 1916, after an ill-advised attempt to make himself emperor, the military-based political fragmentation associated with warlordism became more evident as individual commanders at the head of various military factions began to compete more openly for political power. Nonetheless, the transformation of military commanders into "warlords" was an uneven process that did not coincide exactly with any one date. Some commanders began to exhibit politically independent behavior as early as the Revolution of 1911 (thus a minority view that defines the emergence of warlordism in the political use of military power rather than with political fragmentation, dates the beginning of the warlord period to 1911). In some parts of China this process was slower.

Civil war between competing military coalitions or cliques was the most obvious feature of the warlord period. In 1917-1918, the northern-based Beiyang Army attempted to reassert its control over southern provinces which had declared independence in response to Yuan's monarchical attempt. Over the course of this war, the Beiyang coalition broke into two main cliques, named after the home provinces and main bases of their top leaders: the Anhui Clique led by Duan Qirui, and the Zhili Clique led first by Feng Guozhang and then by Cao Kun and his main subordinate Wu Peifu. Meanwhile, other military factions emerged in the south, the most important being the Yunnan Clique under Tang Jiyao, and the Guangxi Clique of Lu Rongting. The Zhili-Anhui War of 1920 marked the decline of the Anhui Clique and the appearance of a new military power, the Fengtian Clique of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin. Two wars between the Zhili and Fengtian cliques in 1922 and 1924 ultimately resulted in the decline of the Zhili Clique, and the emergence of new power, the Zhili Clique renegade Feng Yuxiang (often referred to as the "Christian general"). Besides major wars between large military coalitions, there were also countless smaller skirmishes between lesser warlords. In some provinces, such as Sichuan, petty warlords with small bases rose and fell in rapid succession. In the other extreme, the military governor of Shanxi province, Yan Xishan, held on to power in his province from 1911 until well beyond the "official" end of the warlord period in 1927. (see plate VIII)

The emergence of warlordism shattered popular hopes that the Revolution of 1911 would pave the way for the creation of a strong and unified Chinese nation. Political and military fragmentation under the warlords hindered China's ability to resist foreign threats. National defense was neglected as military commanders devoted their armies to domestic political struggles. As warlords monopolized state finances to support their growing armies, they deprived the nation of funds needed for educational development and economic construction. Frequent civil wars disrupted agriculture and commerce over wide areas. Thus, although most warlords claimed to be inspired by nationalism, the existence of warlordism became an important obstacle to Chinese nationalist aspirations. As a result, the elimination of warlordism quickly became a central nationalist goal, both for the Guomindang(GMD) and the Chinese Communist Party(CCP).

The success of the Guomindang in defeating the major warlord forces of the time and establishing a new central government in Nanjing (Nanjing Nationalist Government) over a "re-unified" China in 1927 is usually seen as marking the end of the warlord period. Nonetheless, the Guomindang's military success was grounded to a large extent on a strategy of absorbing many warlord forces and their commanders into the Guomindang army. Many of these commanders were granted a considerable degree of political autonomy in their garrison areas as a reward for their support. The result was the continuing existence of what James Sheridan has called "residual warlordism" long after the supposed end of the "Warlord period." Although most individual warlords were eventually pushed from the political scene by the GMD government or their Communist successors, the continuing importance of military power in Chinese politics after 1927 was a legacy of the warlord period. This was true not only for the GMD, where Chiang Kaishek's (Jiang Jieshi) political power on the mainland and on Taiwan had an obvious military foundation, but also for the CCP where the People's Liberation Army has continued to play an extremely important political role. An equally important legacy of the warlord period has been the scar it left on the political consciousness of the Chinese people that reappears periodically in popular fears expressed about any potential recurrence of military-based political fragmentation.
